title: Proxy and Filter/Interceptor Chains
scopeHtml: Scope: Virtual, protection, remote and caching proxies, interceptor chains, Retrofit/OkHttp/Spring examples.

notes.title: Proxy: the idea
notes.html:
A Proxy is a stand-in object with the same interface as the real one, controlling access to it. The client cannot tell the difference. The proxy decides whether, when and how the real call happens.

Mechanism: proxy and real subject implement the same interface; the proxy holds (or lazily creates) the real subject and adds a gate: delay creation, check permission, go over the network, or serve from a cache.

+----------+     +-----------------+
| <<Image>>|<----|  Client         |
| show()   |     +-----------------+
+----+-----+
     ^
 +---+-------------+        has-a / creates lazily
 |                 |  ---------------------------+
RealImage       ImageProxy ------------------------> RealImage
(loads 5 MB)    (cheap, holds path)

The four classic kinds: virtual (lazy creation), protection (access control), remote (hides the network), caching (avoids repeat work). Each gets a section below.

Industry examples. Retrofit create(Api::class.java) returns a java.lang.reflect.Proxy-based object; Hibernate lazy-loaded entities; Spring AOP (@Transactional, @Cacheable) wrap beans in proxies; gRPC client stubs; Android Binder Stub.Proxy for IPC.

Everyday analogy. A receptionist: you talk to them as if they were the director; they decide whether to let you through, take a message, or answer from a notice board.

Decision gravity. Cheap to add behind an interface; reversible. Hard part is that the client no longer sees real costs (network latency, lazy exceptions), so a bad abstraction hides failures. Distinguish clearly from Decorator and Adapter (see the comparison file).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "Proxy and Decorator are the same". Same shape, different intent: Proxy controls ACCESS and often manages the subject's lifecycle; Decorator ADDS behavior.
  • Proxy must have the same interface or the client has to change.

notes.title: Virtual proxy
notes.html:
A virtual proxy delays creating an expensive object until it is really needed. Until the first real use, the proxy is a cheap placeholder.

Worked example. A gallery screen lists 500 photos of 4 MB each. Loading all up front = 2 GB RAM and 10+ s. With virtual proxies each holds just a path (about 100 bytes); only the 8 visible thumbnails load, so about 32 MB and under 300 ms.

interface Image { void show(); }

class RealImage implements Image {
    private final String path;
    RealImage(String path) { this.path = path; System.out.println("loading " + path); }
    public void show() { System.out.println("showing " + path); }
}

class ImageProxy implements Image {
    private final String path;
    private RealImage real;                      // created lazily
    ImageProxy(String path) { this.path = path; }
    public void show() {
        if (real == null) real = new RealImage(path);
        real.show();
    }
}
class ImageProxy(private val path: String) : Image {
    private val real by lazy { RealImage(path) }   // thread-safe lazy by default
    override fun show() = real.show()
}

Before and after. Before: List<RealImage> built in a loop = 500 loads at start. After: List<Image> of proxies = 0 loads at start.

Industry examples. Hibernate lazy associations (the orders list on a User is a proxy collection loaded on first access, and a classic source of LazyInitializationException when the session is closed). Kotlin by lazy. Android Glide placeholders. Spring @Lazy beans.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant menu with photos: the kitchen cooks only what you order, not everything on the menu.

When NOT to use it. If the object is cheap (a 100-byte POJO), if you always need it immediately (lazy adds a branch and hidden latency spike on first use), or if first-use failures would be confusing and must be seen at startup (fail fast).

Common interview traps.

  • Lazy init without thread safety (double creation); use lazy or holder idiom.
  • LazyInitializationException after the session closes.
  • First-request latency spike that load tests did not catch.

notes.title: Protection proxy
notes.html:
A protection proxy checks permissions before forwarding the call. The real object stays free of security code.

Worked example. A DocumentService has read, edit, delete. The proxy holds the caller's role. Role VIEWER: only read passes. A call to delete throws before any I/O. One check class replaces 3 copies of if (role != ADMIN) spread across 30 callers.

interface Documents { String read(String id); void delete(String id); }

class RealDocuments implements Documents {
    public String read(String id) { return "content of " + id; }
    public void delete(String id) { System.out.println("deleted " + id); }
}

class ProtectedDocuments implements Documents {
    enum Role { VIEWER, ADMIN }
    private final Documents real; private final Role role;
    ProtectedDocuments(Documents real, Role role) { this.real = real; this.role = role; }
    public String read(String id) { return real.read(id); }
    public void delete(String id) {
        if (role != Role.ADMIN) throw new SecurityException("forbidden");
        real.delete(id);
    }
}
class ProtectedDocuments(private val real: Documents, private val role: Role) : Documents by real {
    override fun delete(id: String) {
        check(role == Role.ADMIN) { "forbidden" }
        real.delete(id)
    }
}

Industry examples. Spring Security method security (@PreAuthorize) uses proxies. A reverse proxy or API gateway (Nginx, Envoy, Kong) doing authN/authZ in front of services. Collections.unmodifiableList is a read-only guard (proxy-like).

Everyday analogy. A security guard at an office lobby checking badges before the lift.

When NOT to use it. Do not make the proxy your ONLY security layer: anyone who gets the real object bypasses it. Enforce on the server too (defense in depth). Avoid it for fine-grained, data-dependent rules better expressed in the domain model or a policy engine.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a client-side or in-process proxy is real security.
  • Forgetting self-invocation: in Spring AOP, a method calling another method of the same bean skips the proxy.

notes.title: Remote proxy
notes.html:
A remote proxy is a local object that represents an object in another process or machine, hiding the network call. You call a method; the proxy serializes arguments, sends them, waits, and deserializes the answer.

Worked example. weatherApi.forecast("Pune") looks local. The proxy builds GET /v1/forecast?city=Pune, sends it over HTTPS (about 40 to 150 ms round trip), and parses 2 KB of JSON into a Forecast. Time budget: 5 ms serialization + 100 ms network + 5 ms parsing.

// Retrofit generates the remote proxy at runtime
interface WeatherApi {
    @GET("v1/forecast") suspend fun forecast(@Query("city") city: String): Forecast
}
val api = Retrofit.Builder()
    .baseUrl("https://api.example.com/")
    .addConverterFactory(GsonConverterFactory.create())
    .build()
    .create(WeatherApi::class.java)   // a java.lang.reflect.Proxy under the hood
// The JDK mechanism Retrofit relies on
WeatherApi api = (WeatherApi) java.lang.reflect.Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    WeatherApi.class.getClassLoader(),
    new Class<?>[] { WeatherApi.class },
    (proxy, method, args) -> {
        System.out.println("would send HTTP for " + method.getName());
        return null; // real code parses the response
    });

Industry examples. Retrofit services, gRPC stubs, Java RMI, Android Binder AIDL generated Stub.Proxy (cross-process calls), JAX-WS clients.

Everyday analogy. A phone call to a colleague abroad: you speak normally; the phone system carries the words.

When NOT to use it. The "location transparency" idea is dangerous. A remote call can be slow, fail, time out and partially succeed. Pretending it is a local call causes the "fallacies of distributed computing" bugs. Always expose timeouts, retries (with idempotency) and error types; and avoid chatty fine-grained remote interfaces (1000 calls x 50 ms = 50 s).

Common interview traps.

  • Not setting timeouts (OkHttp defaults to 10 s connect/read/write; confirm in docs) and blocking the UI thread.
  • Treating the stub as failure-free.
  • Retrying non-idempotent calls (a payment charged twice).

notes.title: Caching proxy
notes.html:
A caching proxy remembers results of expensive calls and answers repeat requests without touching the real subject.

Worked example. A currency-rate service call takes 120 ms and costs $0.001. The app asks for USD-INR 2,000 times per minute but the rate changes every 60 s. With a 60 s TTL cache, 1 call per minute reaches the service: 99.95% hits, saved 2,000 x 120 ms = 240 s of waiting per minute and $2 per minute.

import java.util.*;

interface Rates { double rate(String pair); }

class CachingRates implements Rates {
    private record Entry(double value, long expiresAt) {}
    private final Rates real; private final long ttlMs;
    private final Map<String, Entry> cache = new java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    CachingRates(Rates real, long ttlMs) { this.real = real; this.ttlMs = ttlMs; }
    public double rate(String pair) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        Entry e = cache.get(pair);
        if (e != null && e.expiresAt() > now) return e.value();
        double v = real.rate(pair);                 // miss: go to the real service
        cache.put(pair, new Entry(v, now + ttlMs));
        return v;
    }
}
class CachingRates(private val real: Rates, private val ttlMs: Long) : Rates {
    private data class Entry(val value: Double, val expiresAt: Long)
    private val cache = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, Entry>()
    override fun rate(pair: String): Double {
        val now = System.currentTimeMillis()
        cache[pair]?.takeIf { it.expiresAt > now }?.let { return it.value }
        return real.rate(pair).also { cache[pair] = Entry(it, now + ttlMs) }
    }
}

Industry examples. CDNs (Cloudflare, CloudFront) and Varnish are caching reverse proxies. OkHttp Cache honours Cache-Control headers. Spring @Cacheable. Hibernate second-level cache.

Everyday analogy. A shopkeeper who remembers today's price list and does not phone the wholesaler for every customer.

When NOT to use it. When data must be strongly fresh (bank balance), when keys are mostly unique (hit rate near 0%, the cache just uses memory), or when invalidation is unclear. Watch for cache stampede: when a hot key expires, 1,000 concurrent callers all miss and hammer the backend; fix with per-key locks, request coalescing, or jittered TTLs. Unbounded caches cause OutOfMemoryError; bound with LRU.

Common interview traps.

  • No invalidation strategy ("there are two hard things...").
  • Check-then-put races causing duplicate backend calls.
  • Caching errors or nulls accidentally.

notes.title: Filter and interceptor chains
notes.html:
A filter (or interceptor) chain passes a request through an ordered list of handlers, each able to act before and after, modify it, or stop it. It is the Decorator/Proxy idea generalized: instead of nesting objects by hand, you register steps and a runner links them (chain of responsibility plus proxy-like gating).

Mechanism: each step receives the request and a chain object; calling chain.proceed(request) runs the rest of the steps and finally the real handler. A step that does not call proceed short-circuits.

 request  -> [Logging] -> [Auth] -> [Cache] -> [Network] 
 response <- [Logging] <- [Auth] <- [Cache] <- [Network]
 Auth failure => returns 401 immediately; Cache and Network never run

Worked example. OkHttp chain: application interceptors (add an Authorization: Bearer header, log), then the cache, retry/redirect, connect, and network interceptors. A request for /profile that a valid cache serves in 2 ms never reaches the network step (about 120 ms).

class AuthInterceptor(private val token: () -> String) : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val request = chain.request().newBuilder()
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer ${token()}")
            .build()
        return chain.proceed(request)          // continue the chain
    }
}
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor { "abc123" })
    .addInterceptor(HttpLoggingInterceptor().apply { level = HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BASIC })
    .build()
// A hand-rolled chain showing the mechanism, runnable on plain Java
import java.util.*;
interface Step { String handle(String req, Chain next); }
class Chain {
    private final List<Step> steps; private final int i;
    Chain(List<Step> steps, int i) { this.steps = steps; this.i = i; }
    String proceed(String req) {
        if (i == steps.size()) return "response to " + req;       // the real handler
        return steps.get(i).handle(req, new Chain(steps, i + 1));
    }
}
// new Chain(List.of(
//   (r, n) -> { System.out.println("log " + r); return n.proceed(r); },
//   (r, n) -> r.contains("token") ? n.proceed(r) : "401"
// ), 0).proceed("GET /x token")

Before and after. Before: every API method adds the auth header, logs, and retries by hand (50 endpoints x 3 concerns = 150 places). After: 3 interceptors register once.

Industry examples. Servlet Filter and Spring HandlerInterceptor; Spring Security filter chain; OkHttp Interceptor; Express/Koa middleware; ASP.NET middleware pipeline; gRPC ClientInterceptor; Envoy HTTP filters.

Everyday analogy. Airport security: ID check, baggage scan, metal detector, in order. Any station can stop you.

Decision gravity. Order is a design decision and a source of bugs; it is easily changed in code but silently breaks behavior (logging before auth logs secrets; retry before cache retries cached results). Treat it like config: document and test the order.

When NOT to use it. For two fixed steps, a direct call is clearer. When business logic hides in interceptors, flow becomes invisible ("magic"). Keep interceptors for cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, metrics, retries, compression), not domain rules.

Common interview traps.

  • Application vs network interceptors in OkHttp: application ones run once per call and see the final response; network ones run per network attempt and see redirects/retries.
  • Forgetting to call proceed (request silently hangs or returns nothing).
  • Reading a response body in a logging interceptor and consuming it so the caller sees an empty body.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Proxy: same interface as the real subject, controls access. Four kinds: virtual (lazy), protection (permissions), remote (network stub), caching (TTL).
  • Real libraries: Retrofit/java.lang.reflect.Proxy, Hibernate lazy loading, Spring AOP, gRPC stubs, Binder, CDNs, OkHttp Cache.
  • Each has a trap: lazy exceptions, proxy-only security, hidden network failures, cache stampede and staleness.
  • Filter/interceptor chains pass a request through ordered steps with proceed(); they handle cross-cutting concerns (auth, logging, retry, cache) and short-circuit when needed. Order matters.
  • Use Proxy for control; use Decorator for adding behavior; use chains for several cross-cutting steps. Do not hide domain logic in interceptors.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Proxy pattern? Name the four classic kinds and one real library example for each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks that you know a proxy is about controlling access, with a same-interface stand-in, and that you can map it to tools you use.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Proxy is a stand-in with the same interface as the real object that controls access to it, so the client cannot tell the difference. Virtual proxy delays creating something expensive (Hibernate lazy loading). Protection proxy checks permissions (Spring Security @PreAuthorize). Remote proxy hides the network (Retrofit service, gRPC stub). Caching proxy answers repeats from memory (OkHttp Cache, @Cacheable).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The proxy and the real subject implement the same interface; the proxy holds the subject or creates it lazily and adds a gate: when, whether, where, or whether at all the real call happens. In Java, java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates such objects at runtime from an interface; Retrofit's create(Api::class.java) uses that.

Client -> Proxy -> (Real subject)

The hard part is that the client no longer sees real costs: latency, network failure, lazy exceptions. A good proxy exposes timeouts and error types.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface Image { void show(); }
class ImageProxy implements Image {
    private final String path; private RealImage real;
    ImageProxy(String path) { this.path = path; }
    public void show() { if (real == null) real = new RealImage(path); real.show(); }
}
class ImageProxy(private val path: String) : Image {
    private val real by lazy { RealImage(path) }          // thread-safe lazy by default
    override fun show() = real.show()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Proxy and Decorator are the same": same shape, different intent (access vs added behavior).
  • Treating a proxy as the only security layer.
  • Hiding remote failures behind a local-looking method.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Retrofit build the object? -> A java.lang.reflect.Proxy whose handler turns method calls into HTTP requests.
  2. Static vs dynamic proxy? -> Static is a hand-written class; dynamic is generated at runtime from the interface.
  3. Which kind needs the most care in production? -> Remote, because of timeouts, retries and partial failures.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the kinds. Senior adds the failure each one hides and the intent test against Decorator and Adapter.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A page rendering 500 photos loaded all images eagerly (2 GB); virtual proxies loaded only the 8 visible ones.

questions.contextHtml:
After a refactor, a REST endpoint that returns a user's orders fails in production but passes in unit tests with mock data.

org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException: failed to lazily initialize a collection of role: User.orders, could not initialize proxy - no Session
  at UserController.toDto(UserController.java:42)
User u = userService.find(id);          // service method is @Transactional; session closes on return
return new UserDto(u.getName(), u.getOrders());   // controller touches the lazy list
questions.promptHtml: Explain the error and give two fixes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch the association to EAGER everywhere," which creates N+1 queries and huge loads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is open-session-in-view on or off? How many orders per user? Does the DTO need all orders?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Load what the endpoint needs inside the service, before the transaction ends.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lazy collection proxy accessed after the session closed; (b) a refactor moved DTO mapping out of the transaction; (c) serialization triggers the lazy load later.
  4. How I'd verify each: The exception names the User.orders proxy and "no Session"; check whether the mapping is outside @Transactional.
  5. Root cause: u.getOrders() returns a virtual proxy; its first access needs an open session to fetch rows.
  6. Fix: Map to the DTO inside the service (the transaction), or fetch with a join (JOIN FETCH) or an entity graph for this use case, or a projection query.
  7. Prevention: an integration test with a real DB and session behavior; do not expose entities to controllers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not enable open-session-in-view as a cure: it holds a connection during view rendering and hides N+1 queries.
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public UserDto findDto(long id) {
    User u = repo.findWithOrders(id);               // JOIN FETCH inside the transaction
    return new UserDto(u.getName(), u.getOrders().stream().map(OrderDto::from).toList());
}
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
fun findDto(id: Long): UserDto {
    val u = repo.findWithOrders(id)                  // JOIN FETCH
    return UserDto(u.name, u.orders.map(OrderDto::from))
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did unit tests pass? -> Mocks use real lists, not Hibernate proxies.
  • Fetching 10,000 orders? -> Paginate; fetching a huge collection defeats the purpose of lazy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an endpoint worked for weeks until a refactor moved mapping out of the transaction and failed only for users with orders.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: marks everything EAGER.
  • Hire: maps inside the transaction or uses join fetch.
  • Strong hire: explains the proxy mechanism, avoids open-session-in-view, adds an integration test.

questions.promptHtml: Proxy, Decorator and Adapter all wrap one object. How do you tell them apart on a code review, and what test would you apply to a wrapper that checks permissions?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Pattern naming is only useful when it tells you what the class must and must not do.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The test is interface and intent. Adapter exposes a different interface than it wraps to make things fit. Decorator exposes the same interface and adds behavior. Proxy exposes the same interface and controls access to the subject: lazy creation, permission, remote call, cache. A wrapper that checks permissions before forwarding is a Proxy, because its job is to gate the call, not to add a feature.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A decorator is usually built by the caller around an object it already has (new Buffered(src)); a proxy often creates or locates the real subject itself, and may never call it. The same FileSource can be adapted to Reader, decorated with timing, or proxied to open lazily for admins only.

Adapter  : Client -> TargetIface   -> Adapter   -> Adaptee (other iface)
Decorator: Client -> SameIface     -> Decorator -> Component
Proxy    : Client -> SameIface     -> Proxy     -> RealSubject (may not call it)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

class ProtectedDocuments implements Documents {          // Proxy: may refuse to call real
    public void delete(String id) { if (role != Role.ADMIN) throw new SecurityException("forbidden"); real.delete(id); }
}
class ProtectedDocuments(private val real: Documents, private val role: Role) : Documents by real {
    override fun delete(id: String) { check(role == Role.ADMIN) { "forbidden" }; real.delete(id) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling an access check a Decorator.
  • A "decorator" that also owns the lifecycle of the subject (it is a proxy).
  • Assuming same UML means same pattern.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Retrofit a proxy or adapter? -> The service object is a proxy; CallAdapter is an adapter; interceptors are decorator-like.
  2. Does it matter in practice? -> It tells the next dev what belongs inside: access and lifecycle vs extra behavior vs translation.
  3. Can one class be two? -> Yes, but then split it; mixed intent grows into a god wrapper.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "same thing". Senior applies the interface-and-intent test and names an example of each in the code base.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "logging decorator" that also skipped calls for unauthorized users was untested as a security control and let a path through.

questions.contextHtml:
A Spring service secures an admin action with a method annotation. An audit finds that a normal user could trigger the refund through the public export endpoint.

@Service
class RefundService {
    public void bulkExport(List<String> ids) {          // no security annotation
        for (String id : ids) refund(id);                // internal call
    }
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public void refund(String id) { /* moves money */ }
}

Calling refundService.refund("x") from a controller as a normal user is correctly rejected with 403.
questions.promptHtml: Why does bulkExport bypass the check and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The annotation is broken" or "add the annotation to every method" without explaining the proxy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Proxy mode (JDK or CGLIB) or AspectJ weaving? Which roles may call bulkExport?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on bulkExport now and review exposure.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) refund is called through this, not through the Spring proxy; (b) the endpoint is unauthenticated; (c) role mapping bug.
  4. How I'd verify each: Direct calls get 403 but the export path does not; debug and print AopUtils.isAopProxy(this), which is false inside the class.
  5. Root cause: Spring AOP security is a protection proxy around the bean. The check runs only on calls that enter through the proxy; this.refund() skips it.
  6. Fix: Put the authorization at the entry point that is exposed (bulkExport) and/or move refund into a separate bean injected into RefundService, so the call goes through its proxy. Authorize at the web layer too.
  7. Prevention: security tests for every entry point with each role; an ArchUnit or review rule that secured methods are not called internally.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on a method proxy alone. Enforce in the domain or data layer too (defense in depth). AspectJ weaving fixes self-invocation but adds build complexity.
@Service class RefundService {
    private final RefundExecutor executor;                // another bean, calls go via proxy
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    public void bulkExport(List<String> ids) { ids.forEach(executor::refund); }
}
@Service
class RefundService(private val executor: RefundExecutor) {
    @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
    fun bulkExport(ids: List<String>) = ids.forEach(executor::refund)
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does it work from the controller? -> The controller holds the proxy bean, not the target.
  • Does private + annotation help? -> No; private methods are not intercepted by proxy-based AOP.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a payment-approval flow guarded by an annotation was bypassed through an internal batch method for months before an audit sampled the call paths.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: re-adds annotations randomly.
  • Hire: explains self-invocation and restructures through another bean.
  • Strong hire: defense in depth, entry-point authorization and per-role tests.

questions.promptHtml: A remote proxy such as a Retrofit interface makes a network call look like a local method. What are the risks of that illusion and how do you design around them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks that you know the fallacies of distributed computing and can turn them into API design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A remote call can be slow, fail, time out, or succeed without the caller knowing, so treating it as a local call causes bugs. I set explicit timeouts, return a result type or error types, retry only idempotent calls (with an idempotency key for writes), keep calls off the UI thread, and avoid chatty fine-grained interfaces because 1,000 calls at 50 ms is 50 seconds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cost model for forecast("Pune"): about 5 ms serialization + about 100 ms network + about 5 ms parsing. Failure modes: DNS, connect timeout, read timeout, 5xx, partial success (server committed, response lost). OkHttp's default timeouts are 10 s for connect, read and write (verify in the docs of your version); a hung server then blocks a thread for 10 s.

App -> Stub (proxy) -> serialize -> network -> server -> response lost?
Unknown outcome: did the charge happen?

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

OkHttpClient client = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).readTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3)).callTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build();
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS).readTimeout(3, TimeUnit.SECONDS).callTimeout(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS).build()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No timeouts or the default on a UI path.
  • Retrying a non-idempotent POST (charges twice).
  • Returning null or a plain value so callers forget the failure case.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you make a POST safely retryable? -> Send an idempotency key; the server returns the first result for repeats.
  2. Why avoid chatty interfaces? -> Latency multiplies per call; batch or coarsen.
  3. Where do timeouts belong? -> At the client per call, plus a total deadline; the server also needs its own.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "handle exceptions". Senior covers unknown outcomes, idempotency, deadlines and chatty-call math.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mobile app called a stub on the main thread with a 10 s default timeout; slow networks produced ANRs.

class CachingRates implements Rates {
    private final Rates real; private final long ttlMs;
    public double rate(String pair) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();            // hidden dependency on the clock
        /* ... */
    }

questions.promptHtml: Make it testable and describe the tests that matter.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Thread.sleep with a smaller TTL in test and a real service call.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should errors be cached? Is the cache shared across threads? What is the max size?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the 61-second sleep test from the PR gate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Not a bug, a testability problem: time and the real service are hidden dependencies.
  4. How I'd verify each: After the change tests must run in milliseconds with no network.
  5. Root cause: System.currentTimeMillis hard-coded in the class.
  6. Fix: Inject a LongSupplier (or Clock), and a counting fake Rates. Tests: (1) two calls inside the TTL hit the fake once; (2) advance the fake clock past TTL, the fake is hit again; (3) different pairs are cached separately; (4) a thrown exception is not cached.
  7. Prevention: ban direct System.currentTimeMillis in business classes; a stampede test with threads.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not mock a static clock; an injected supplier is simpler.
class CachingRates implements Rates {
    private record Entry(double value, long expiresAt) {}
    private final Rates real; private final long ttlMs; private final LongSupplier clock;
    private final Map<String, Entry> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    CachingRates(Rates real, long ttlMs, LongSupplier clock) { this.real = real; this.ttlMs = ttlMs; this.clock = clock; }
    public double rate(String pair) {
        long now = clock.getAsLong();
        Entry e = cache.get(pair);
        if (e != null && e.expiresAt() > now) return e.value();
        double v = real.rate(pair);
        cache.put(pair, new Entry(v, now + ttlMs));
        return v;
    }
}
// test: long[] t = {0}; new CachingRates(fake, 60_000, () -> t[0]); t[0] = 61_000 -> real called again
class CachingRates(private val real: Rates, private val ttlMs: Long, private val clock: () -> Long) : Rates {
    private data class Entry(val value: Double, val expiresAt: Long)
    private val cache = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, Entry>()
    override fun rate(pair: String): Double {
        val now = clock()
        cache[pair]?.takeIf { it.expiresAt > now }?.let { return it.value }
        return real.rate(pair).also { cache[pair] = Entry(it, now + ttlMs) }
    }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two threads miss at once. -> Duplicate backend calls; test with a latch and fix with per-key loading.
  • What about a null or failed response? -> Do not cache errors unless deliberately with a short TTL.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a 60-second sleep test was marked flaky and skipped, and a later refactor broke expiry so rates stayed stale for hours.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sleeps in tests.
  • Hire: injects clock and fake and tests hit, expiry, miss.
  • Strong hire: also tests error non-caching and concurrency.

questions.contextHtml:
A CachingRates proxy (TTL 60 s) fronts a pricing service that handles 400 rps at most. Every minute on the minute, the pricing service melts for a few seconds.

12:00:00 cache expires for key USD-INR
12:00:00.0-0.9  pricing-service rps: 410  p99: 9.8 s  errors: 31%
12:00:01  recovered
app: 1,800 rps on USD-INR across 40 pods, each pod has its own cache
questions.promptHtml: Explain the pattern, name the fixes in order, and say what you would not do.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the TTL." That moves the spike later and makes data staler.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How stale may the rate be? Is the key set small and hot? Is a shared cache available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Serve stale for a few seconds while one request refreshes; add jitter to TTL; rate-limit the backend caller.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stampede: all callers miss at expiry and call the backend at once; (b) 40 pods multiply the herd; (c) backend capacity too small (red herring: it handles normal load).
  4. How I'd verify each: Backend request rate by minute second; cache hit rate drop exactly at expiry; per-pod logs of simultaneous misses.
  5. Root cause: Synchronized expiry with no request coalescing: after expiry, every concurrent caller goes to the real subject.
  6. Fix: Per-key single-flight: one thread loads while others wait or use the stale value. Add TTL jitter (for example 60 s plus or minus 10%) and refresh-ahead before expiry; consider a shared cache tier or a small L1 plus shared L2.
  7. Prevention: a load test around expiry; a dashboard of backend QPS by cause; alert on cache hit-rate dips.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Serving stale increases staleness risk, which is fine for rates but not for balances. I would not raise TTL blindly or add backend replicas as the only fix.
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<Double>> inflight = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
public double rate(String pair) {
    Entry e = cache.get(pair);
    if (e != null && e.expiresAt() > now()) return e.value();
    CompletableFuture<Double> f = inflight.computeIfAbsent(pair,
        k -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> real.rate(k)));        // single flight
    try { double v = f.join(); cache.put(pair, new Entry(v, now() + jitteredTtl())); return v; }
    finally { inflight.remove(pair, f); }
}
private val inflight = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<Double>>()
override fun rate(pair: String): Double {
    cache[pair]?.takeIf { it.expiresAt > now() }?.let { return it.value }
    val f = inflight.computeIfAbsent(pair) { CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { real.rate(it) } }
    return try { f.join().also { cache[pair] = Entry(it, now() + jitteredTtl()) } } finally { inflight.remove(pair, f) }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The loader fails. -> Complete the future exceptionally, do not cache the failure for long, and keep serving stale if allowed.
  • Single-flight across 40 pods? -> Use a distributed lock or a shared cache with a short lease; in-process single-flight reduces 1,800 to 40 calls.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a minute-aligned TTL produced a periodic backend brownout until jitter and single-flight were added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer TTL.
  • Hire: single-flight and jitter.
  • Strong hire: stale-while-revalidate, distributed herd reasoning and a test around expiry.

questions.contextHtml:
An OkHttp client is built like this. After release, a security scan finds bearer tokens in logs, and the backend sees duplicate POST /orders requests whenever it answers 503.

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor { token })
    .addInterceptor(HttpLoggingInterceptor().apply { level = HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.HEADERS })
    .addInterceptor(RetryInterceptor(maxAttempts = 3))
    .cache(Cache(cacheDir, 10L * 1024 * 1024))
    .build()
INFO  --> GET /profile
INFO  Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...   <- token in logs
questions.promptHtml: Explain the symptoms in terms of order and fix the chain.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set the log level to NONE in production" and leave the rest.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should retries be per call or per attempt? Which endpoints are idempotent? Do we want to log headers at all?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Redact Authorization in the logging interceptor; rotate exposed tokens.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) logging sits after auth and runs at HEADERS level, so it prints the Authorization header it now sees; (b) the retry interceptor applies to every method, including POST; (c) a second logger at network level (red herring, check it anyway).
  4. How I'd verify each: Print client.interceptors and client.networkInterceptors; compare the logs.
  5. Root cause: Order was never specified or tested, and logging was configured to print sensitive headers. Interceptors run in registration order, so logging after auth sees the secret; and the retry step re-issues any request on 503 without checking the method is idempotent.
  6. Fix: Use redactHeader("Authorization") on the logging interceptor. Keep a deliberate order (auth, then logging with redaction) and place retry deliberately: only retry idempotent requests, with backoff, and not on 4xx. Let OkHttp's built-in retry handle connection failures.
  7. Prevention: a unit test that builds the client through one factory and asserts interceptor order and redaction; a log-scrubbing rule.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not log bodies in production; headers only with redaction. Retry in an interceptor can double-send writes; restrict by method and idempotency key.
val logging = HttpLoggingInterceptor().apply {
    level = HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BASIC
    redactHeader("Authorization")
}
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor { token })
    .addInterceptor(logging)
    .addInterceptor(RetryInterceptor(maxAttempts = 3, retryOn = { it.method == "GET" }))
    .cache(Cache(cacheDir, 10L * 1024 * 1024))
    .build()
HttpLoggingInterceptor logging = new HttpLoggingInterceptor();
logging.setLevel(HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BASIC);
logging.redactHeader("Authorization");
OkHttpClient client = new OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(new AuthInterceptor(() -> token))
    .addInterceptor(logging)
    .cache(new Cache(cacheDir, 10L * 1024 * 1024)).build();

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Where does the cache sit relative to application interceptors? -> Application interceptors run before the cache layer, so they run once per call even for a cache hit; network interceptors do not run on a hit.
  • Want a log of what actually went on the wire? -> Add a network interceptor (sees redirects and retries).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: HEADERS-level logging shipped tokens to a third-party log SaaS for two weeks until a scan flagged them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: turns logging off.
  • Hire: redacts and sets a deliberate order.
  • Strong hire: separates application and network interceptors, restricts retry to idempotent calls and pins order in a test.

questions.subtopic: Double charge through a retry proxy
questions.contextHtml:
A mobile app uses a Retrofit service for payments. On poor networks some users report two charges. Server logs:

POST /charge  order=9921  t=0.0s   -> processed, response lost (client read timeout at 3s)
POST /charge  order=9921  t=3.1s   -> processed again
interface PaymentsApi { @POST("charge") suspend fun charge(@Body req: ChargeRequest): ChargeResponse }
// client: retryOnConnectionFailure(true), custom RetryInterceptor(maxAttempts = 3) on all methods

Support counts about 60 double charges in a week out of 40,000 payments.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure, stop the bleeding and fix it end to end.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the read timeout to 30 s." It reduces frequency but not the root cause, and hurts UX.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the server support an idempotency key? Are charges already deduplicated by order id? What is the p99 server latency?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable client retries for POST /charge; refund duplicates (list by order id with two successes).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the first request succeeded but the response was lost, then retried; (b) server is slow so timeouts hit often (red herring if p99 is 400 ms); (c) user double-tapped the button.
  4. How I'd verify each: Same order id twice with 3.1 s gap in logs means retry, not double tap (taps are typically within 300 ms and share a client request id).
  5. Root cause: The remote proxy made a non-idempotent call look retryable. The outcome was unknown, not failed.
  6. Fix: Add an Idempotency-Key (UUID per payment attempt, stored with the order) that the server uses to return the first result for repeats. Keep retries but only with the key. On timeout show "checking payment status" and query the order by id.
  7. Prevention: a chaos test that drops responses after the server commits; metrics on duplicate keys; a client test that POSTs have keys.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not retry blind; I would not rely on a client disabling the button as the only guard.
interface PaymentsApi {
    @POST("charge") suspend fun charge(
        @Header("Idempotency-Key") key: String, @Body req: ChargeRequest): ChargeResponse
}
// key = persisted per order attempt, reused on every retry of the same attempt
interface PaymentsApi {
    @POST("charge") Call<ChargeResponse> charge(@Header("Idempotency-Key") String key, @Body ChargeRequest req);
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Server stores keys for how long? -> Long enough for realistic retries (hours to days); verify the provider's policy.
  • Key reuse with a different body? -> Reject with 409/422; same key must mean the same request.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a weekly handful of double charges traced to an interceptor retrying POSTs; idempotency keys fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: longer timeout.
  • Hire: stops POST retries and adds an idempotency key.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes unknown outcome from failure, adds status query, chaos test and refund plan.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate adds a "log the response body" interceptor. After release, JSON parsing fails randomly and an IllegalStateException: closed shows up in crash reports for only some requests.

class BodyLogger : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val response = chain.proceed(chain.request())
        Log.d("HTTP", response.body!!.string())     // consumes the stream
        return response                              // caller now gets a closed body
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does it break callers and how do you write it correctly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in try/catch" or "log asynchronously".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How large are the bodies? Is this needed in production or only debug builds? Do bodies contain PII?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the interceptor in release builds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) body.string() reads and closes the one-shot stream; (b) multiple interceptors both read; (c) a large body is being buffered in memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with a single request; ResponseBody can only be read once.
  5. Root cause: A response body is a one-shot stream; the interceptor consumed it before the caller.
  6. Fix: Use response.peekBody(maxBytes) to read a copy of up to a limit without consuming the original, or use the built-in HttpLoggingInterceptor at a debug-only level.
  7. Prevention: a code-review rule for interceptors: never read the real body; tests that the caller can still parse the response after the chain.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: peekBody buffers up to the limit; set it small (for example 4 KB). I would not log bodies in production because of PII and cost.
class BodyLogger : Interceptor {
    override fun intercept(chain: Interceptor.Chain): Response {
        val response = chain.proceed(chain.request())
        Log.d("HTTP", response.peekBody(4 * 1024).string())    // copy, original untouched
        return response
    }
}
public Response intercept(Chain chain) throws IOException {
    Response response = chain.proceed(chain.request());
    Log.d("HTTP", response.peekBody(4 * 1024).string());
    return response;
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Streaming bodies? -> peekBody waits for bytes up to the limit; for streams skip logging.
  • A request body? -> Same issue with one-shot request bodies; use a Buffer copy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a debug logger left on in a release build emptied every response body for 5% of users on a single endpoint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swallows the exception.
  • Hire: peekBody or the stock logger.
  • Strong hire: explains one-shot streams, PII and release-build policy.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how an interceptor chain works internally, how a step short-circuits, and the difference between OkHttp application and network interceptors.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you understand proceed() as recursion and can reason about order and placement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each step receives the request and a chain object. Calling chain.proceed(request) runs the rest of the steps and finally the real handler, then control returns back up so each step can act on the response. A step that does not call proceed short-circuits, for example an auth step returning 401. In OkHttp, application interceptors run once per call and see the final response; network interceptors run per network attempt and see redirects and retries, and do not run when the cache answers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
It is Decorator generalized, plus Chain of Responsibility: registering ordered steps replaces hand-nested wrappers. Mechanically, the chain is an index into a list; proceed builds a chain for index + 1, so the call stack is the pipeline.

request  -> [Logging] -> [Auth] -> [Cache] -> [Network]
response <- [Logging] <- [Auth] <- [Cache] <- [Network]
Auth failure => 401 returned immediately; Cache and Network never run

Order is behavior: logging before auth hides the header; retry before cache retries cached results.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface Step { String handle(String req, Chain next); }
class Chain {
    private final List<Step> steps; private final int i;
    Chain(List<Step> s, int i) { steps = s; this.i = i; }
    String proceed(String req) {
        return i == steps.size() ? "response to " + req : steps.get(i).handle(req, new Chain(steps, i + 1));
    }
}
fun interface Step { fun handle(req: String, next: Chain): String }
class Chain(private val steps: List<Step>, private val i: Int = 0) {
    fun proceed(req: String): String =
        if (i == steps.size) "response to $req" else steps[i].handle(req, Chain(steps, i + 1))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to call proceed (the request hangs or returns nothing).
  • Reading the response body and consuming it.
  • Putting domain logic in interceptors so flow becomes invisible.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where would you put metrics? -> Outermost application interceptor for per-call latency; a network interceptor for per-attempt timings.
  2. Servlet equivalents? -> Filter with FilterChain.doFilter; Spring HandlerInterceptor.
  3. How do you test the order? -> Build the chain through one factory and assert a recorded sequence with a fake at the end.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "it is a list of handlers". Senior explains proceed recursion, short-circuiting, and application vs network placement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cache placed after an auth step stored responses keyed without the user token, leaking one user's data to another.

questions.contextHtml:
A report screen shares one ReportProxy per report across request threads. The real report loads a 300 MB dataset on first use. After a traffic spike the heap hits 3.4 GB and logs show:

INFO loading dataset for report 77 (thread http-12)
INFO loading dataset for report 77 (thread http-19)
INFO loading dataset for report 77 (thread http-31)
GC overhead: 3 x 300 MB live copies of report 77
class ReportProxy implements Report {
    private RealReport real;                         // lazy
    public Data data() {
        if (real == null) real = new RealReport(id); // 300 MB load, 4 s
        return real.data();
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain the bug and give a fix that loads once, with the trade-offs of each option.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make data() synchronized." That works but locks every read for the proxy's life.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the proxy truly shared? Does load failure need retry? Should the dataset ever be evicted?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-load the hottest reports at startup; restart with a bigger heap only as a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-act race creates several copies; (b) real has no visibility guarantee; (c) a memory leak elsewhere (the three identical load lines argue against it).
  4. How I'd verify each: Three load logs within 4 s for the same id; a test with a CountDownLatch releasing 20 threads at once and counting constructor calls.
  5. Root cause: Unsynchronized lazy initialization of a shared field.
  6. Fix: Kotlin by lazy (synchronized by default); in Java the holder idiom or Suppliers.memoize-style memoization, or a volatile field with double-checked locking. If load can fail, make sure a failure is not cached forever.
  7. Prevention: a concurrent init test counting constructions; review rule: lazy fields on shared objects must use a safe idiom.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A full synchronized method is simplest but serializes every read. Double-checked locking needs volatile. With 300 MB objects I would also add eviction, otherwise the lazy cache is a leak.
class ReportProxy implements Report {
    private volatile RealReport real;
    public Data data() {
        RealReport r = real;
        if (r == null) {
            synchronized (this) {
                r = real;
                if (r == null) real = r = new RealReport(id);
            }
        }
        return r.data();
    }
}
class ReportProxy(private val id: Long) : Report {
    private val real by lazy { RealReport(id) }      // synchronized: loads once, concurrent callers wait
    override fun data() = real.data()
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The load throws. -> by lazy rethrows and retries on the next call; with hand-written code do not store a half-built object.
  • 4 s block for the second caller is too long. -> Return a loading state or load asynchronously and serve a placeholder.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a lazily loaded dataset was built three times in parallel after a deploy; the first-request spike used triple the memory and tripped OOM.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: synchronizes everything or ignores visibility.
  • Hire: safe lazy idiom and a test counting initializations.
  • Strong hire: addresses failure caching, eviction and the 4 s wait experience.
